The [Modulo Calculator](/modulo-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Remainder and modulo of any division — a mod b, with quotient. Enter your dividend (a) and divisor (b) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

The modulo operation finds the remainder left over after division. 17 mod 5 is 2, because 5 goes into 17 three times (15) with 2 left over. Modulo is everywhere in computing: it wraps values into a range (clocks use mod 12 and mod 60), tests whether a number is even or odd, cycles through array indexes, and powers hash functions and cryptography. This calculator shows both the remainder and the floored modulo, which differ for negative numbers.

## How to use the Modulo Calculator

Start by entering your dividend (a), then entering your divisor (b). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the dividend — the number being divided.
2. Enter the divisor — the number you divide by.
3. Read the remainder, the floored modulo and the quotient.

## Formula

a = q × b + r, where q is the truncated quotient and r the remainder (0 ≤ |r| < |b|). The floored modulo is ((a % b) + b) % b, which is always non-negative when b is positive.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Modulo Calculator](/modulo-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. 17 mod 5 = 2 (17 = 3 × 5 + 2). −17 mod 5 = 3 as a floored modulo, while the remainder is −2 — the two agree for positive numbers and differ for negative ones. Try the same figures in the [Modulo Calculator](/modulo-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Dividend (a): 17, Divisor (b): 5), the [Modulo Calculator](/modulo-calculator) returns Remainder (a % b): 2, Modulo (floored): 2, Quotient: 3, Check: 17 = 3 × 5 + 2. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Remainder vs modulo

Most programming languages use % for the remainder, which keeps the sign of the dividend: −17 % 5 is −2. The mathematical modulo (floored) is always non-negative for a positive divisor: −17 mod 5 is 3. For positive numbers the two are identical, so the difference only matters with negative dividends. If you are writing code that wraps an index or a clock, you almost always want the floored modulo.

## Where modulo is used

Clocks are modulo 12, minutes are modulo 60, and days of the week are modulo 7. In programming, x % 2 tests evenness, x % 10 gives the last digit, and hash tables use modulo to turn a hash into a bucket index. Cryptography leans on it heavily: RSA encryption is arithmetic modulo a large number.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- a mod b is always between 0 and b − 1 (for positive b) — use it to wrap values into a range.
- To test if a divides b exactly, check whether b mod a is 0.
- For negative dividends, decide whether you need the remainder or the floored modulo before coding.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is modulo?

The remainder after division. 17 mod 5 is 2 because 5 × 3 = 15 and 17 − 15 = 2. It answers 'what is left over?' rather than 'how many times does it go in?' Try it with your own numbers in the [Modulo Calculator](/modulo-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the difference between remainder and modulo?

For positive numbers they are the same. For negative dividends they differ: −17 % 5 is −2 as a remainder, but 3 as a floored modulo. This calculator shows both. Try it with your own numbers in the [Modulo Calculator](/modulo-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Can you divide by zero?

No — division by zero is undefined, so the calculator refuses it. The modulo of any number by zero has no meaningful value. Try it with your own numbers in the [Modulo Calculator](/modulo-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
